title: Nehemiah 8:1–6
context: With the wall finished and the people settled in their towns (Nehemiah 7:73), all the people gather as one man in the wide place before the water gate on the first day of the seventh month and ask Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses. Ezra reads from early morning until midday to men, women, and all who could understand, standing on a wooden platform with thirteen men beside him, while the people listen attentively, stand when the book is opened, answer Amen, Amen, and bow in worship. The scene echoes earlier public readings of the law (compare Deuteronomy 31:10–12; Joshua 8:35; 2 Kings 23:2). The names beside Ezra in verse 4 do not match other lists exactly, and they are best read as given. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about the central place of God’s word in the life of his people and reverent, attentive hearing.

verses.text: All the people gathered themselves together as one man into the wide place that was in front of the water gate; and they spoke to Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded to Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see all the people gathering as one man and asking Ezra to bring the book of the law. The desire to hear God’s word comes from the people themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the people’s hunger for the law as a sign of God at work among them. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of a community gathered around Scripture.

verses.text: Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly, both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding, on the first day of the seventh month.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezra bringing the law before men, women, and all who could understand, on the first day of the seventh month. The word is for the whole community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusive assembly as reflecting the law’s own call to gather all the people (compare Deuteronomy 31:12). Both traditions commonly read the verse as honoring every hearer.

verses.text: He read from it before the wide place that was in front of the water gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women, and of those who could understand. The ears of all the people were attentive to the book of the law.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezra reading from early morning until midday, with all the people attentive. Patient, sustained listening marks a hungry heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the attentive ears as the fitting response to God speaking through his word (compare Romans 10:17). Readers in both traditions commonly hold up the verse as a model of reverent hearing.

verses.text: Ezra the scribe stood on a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezra standing on a wooden platform with thirteen men beside him. The arrangement helps everyone see and hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shared platform as showing that the reading was a public, accountable act. Both traditions commonly read the names as given, without forcing them to match other lists.

verses.text: Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people (for he was above all the people), and when he opened it, all the people stood up.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezra opening the book in the sight of all, and the people standing. Reverence is shown in posture as well as heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the standing as honor given to God, whose word is being opened. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of respect for Scripture.

verses.text: Then Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God. All the people answered, “Amen, Amen,” with the lifting up of their hands. They bowed their heads, and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezra blessing the LORD, and the people answering Amen, Amen, lifting their hands and bowing in worship. Hearing leads naturally to worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the response as wholehearted agreement with God’s word and praise of his greatness. Both traditions commonly read the verse as joining word and worship together.
